stem: Name the six foundational architectures of this course, in order from predictive to generative.
choices: Perceptron, MLP, CNN, RNN, LSTM, Transformer
MLP, CNN, VAE, U-Net, Transformer, Diffusion
MLP, CNN, GAN, VAE, Transformer, Diffusion
CNN, RNN, GAN, VAE, U-Net, Transformer
explanation: MLP, CNN, VAE, U-Net, Transformer, Diffusion. MLP and CNN predict, VAE and U-Net form the representation bridge, and Transformer and Diffusion generate — the GAN is part of the story but not one of the six.

stem: The six architectures are grouped into three stages, each with its own question. Which set of questions is right?
choices: 'What is it?' for prediction, 'what is it made of?' for the bridge, 'what is it worth?' for generation
'What was?' for prediction, 'what is?' for the bridge, 'what will be?' for generation
'What is most likely?' for predictive AI, 'what is the underlying structure?' for the representation bridge, 'what could be?' for generative AI
'How accurate?' for prediction, 'how compressed?' for the bridge, 'how creative?' for generation
explanation: Predict what is most likely, represent the underlying structure, generate what could be. The same core idea — a network learning useful representations — powers all three; each stage only adds a capability.

stem: This course defines generative AI as a system that does what?
choices: Captures the underlying probability distribution of a dataset in order to synthesise new samples that appear to come from the same distribution
Produces output no human has ever thought of before
Combines several trained models so their outputs can be averaged
Answers any question put to it in natural language
explanation: Capture the distribution, then synthesise from it. That definition covers text, images and audio at once, and it is what makes 'plausible context relevance' the right standard: a new sample cannot be checked against a ground truth that does not exist.

stem: What is a GAN, and how do its two networks relate?
choices: A Generalised Adaptive Network, in which one network adapts the learning rate of the other
A Generative Adversarial Network: a generator produces fakes and a discriminator judges real against fake, and both improve by playing against each other
A Grouped Attention Network, in which attention heads are split into competing groups
A Generative Autoencoder Network, in which the encoder and decoder are trained separately
explanation: Generator against discriminator, each one's improvement raising the bar for the other. The training signal is not a label but the opponent's judgement, which is what makes it adversarial.

stem: What is ironic about the GAN's place in the history of generative AI?
choices: It was invented twice independently and neither team was credited
It generates images but was designed for text
It was proposed as a joke at a conference and later taken seriously
The adversarial setup was devised as a device for sharpening a predictive, discriminative model — and the generator, the supporting act, turned out to be the star
explanation: The point of the generator was to give the discriminator harder cases to learn from. Deepfakes made the generator famous instead, and 'generative' took on its modern meaning from this architecture before GPT inherited the word.

stem: In a GAN, one network makes the fakes. One word: what is the other one called, the one that judges real against fake?
explanation: The discriminator. It is an ordinary predictive classifier — real or fake — and the generator learns purely from how well it fools it, with no direct target image to copy.

stem: A GAN and a VAE both end up producing new images. What is the difference in how each is trained?
choices: The GAN learns from the judgement of a second network it is competing with; the VAE learns from reconstructing its own inputs while keeping its latent space close to a simple distribution
The GAN learns from labelled images; the VAE learns from unlabelled ones
The GAN adds noise to the data and learns to remove it; the VAE does the reverse
The GAN is trained once; the VAE must be retrained for every new image it generates
explanation: Different learning games with the same end. The GAN has no reconstruction target at all, only an opponent's verdict; the VAE never sees an opponent, only its own reconstruction error and a pull towards a simple latent prior.

stem: How does a diffusion model generate an image?
choices: It assembles the image from fragments of the training images that best match the prompt
It encodes the prompt into a latent point and decodes it in a single step
A fixed forward process gradually corrupts data with noise; the model learns to reverse that, so generation starts from pure noise and iteratively denoises, optionally guided by a text embedding
It grows the image outward from a seed pixel, predicting each neighbour in turn
explanation: Destroy, then learn to undo. Because the corruption was applied deliberately, the true noise at every step is known, which turns generation into an ordinary supervised problem repeated many times over.

stem: In a diffusion model, which direction is learned and which is prescribed?
choices: The forward noising is learned; the reverse denoising is prescribed by a fixed schedule
Both directions are learned, one after the other
Neither is learned; both are fixed, and only the sampling temperature is trained
The forward noising is prescribed — it is designed, not learned — and only the reverse denoising is learned
explanation: The forward process is designed, so the true noise added at each step is known exactly. That known answer is the supervision for the reverse, which is the only part the network learns.

stem: One word: what does a diffusion model start from when it generates a brand-new image?
explanation: Noise — a field of pure Gaussian randomness. The model then removes a little of it at a time, and after many steps what is left is a sample from the data distribution rather than a copy of anything in the training set.

stem: VAE, diffusion and flow matching are presented as one family. What is the unifying view?
choices: All three are autoencoders; only the size of the bottleneck differs
All three are trained adversarially against a discriminator
All three are different learning games with the same goal: a learnable mapping from a simple distribution to the data distribution, which you then sample by cranking a random number generator
All three require labelled training data and differ only in the label format
explanation: Same destination, three routes. Each one constructs a mapping between a simple distribution and the data, turns that into a supervised learning task, and generates by sampling the simple distribution and applying what it learned.

stem: Flow matching is the third member of that family. In one line, what does it do?
choices: It matches each generated sample against the closest training example and corrects the difference

It defines a probability path from a simple distribution to the data and learns the vector field that transports samples along it, so generation means starting from noise and following the learned flow
It matches the output of several generators and averages them
It flows gradients backwards through time, as a recurrent network does
explanation: A path plus a velocity field along it. Diffusion takes many discrete denoising steps; flow matching learns a continuous transport instead, but the goal — noise in, data out — is identical.

stem: Can we have generative AI without neural networks?
choices: No — generation requires a learned representation, which only a neural network can hold
No — sampling from a distribution is statistics, not generation

Yes in principle: a Markov chain generates text from next-token statistics, and any sampler from a fitted distribution is generative. But without a learned representation it has no context, so the output is locally plausible and globally incoherent
Yes, and the output is indistinguishable from a neural model's, only slower to produce
explanation: Yes on the definition, no in practice. Generation only needs a fitted distribution you can sample from; what the neural network adds is context, which is the difference between plausible phrases and a coherent paragraph.

stem: A text-to-image model is given the prompt 'a cat wearing sunglasses'. Where does the prompt enter a diffusion model?
choices: It is embedded and used to condition the denoising at every step, so each step is steered towards images matching the description
It is used to search the training set for images with matching captions, which are then blended
It is applied once at the end, to select the best image from a batch of candidates
It replaces the initial noise, which is generated from the text instead of at random
explanation: Conditioning. The prompt is turned into an embedding that the reverse process consults at every denoising step, which is why the image steadily converges on the description rather than towards any picture at all.

stem: A team needs to write product descriptions, and another needs to create product photographs that were never shot. Which architectures fit, and why?
choices: A transformer for both, because attention handles any modality
A U-Net for the text and a CNN for the images, because both preserve detail
A GAN for the text and a VAE for the images, because both are adversarial
A transformer for the text, because it models long-range dependencies in sequences, and a diffusion model for the images, because it turns randomness into high-quality realistic pictures
explanation: Sequence generation is the transformer's task and high-quality image generation is the diffusion model's. They are the two generative architectures of the six, and their typical tasks are what separates them.

stem: In what sense is the diffusion model described as coming out of the transformer story and being 'for visuals'?
choices: A diffusion model is a transformer with the attention layers removed
Diffusion models were first published as a chapter of the transformer paper
The two are unrelated; the diffusion model descends only from the autoencoder
Diffusion carries the generative turn across from language to images, and modern text-to-image systems use a text transformer to embed the prompt that conditions the denoising network
explanation: The lineage is about where generation went next, not about layers. Language got there first through the transformer; diffusion did the same job for pixels, and it leans on a text encoder whenever the image has to match a prompt.

stem: A diffusion model learns both the process that adds noise to an image and the process that removes it.
choices: True
False
explanation: False. The noising process is prescribed and fixed, which is exactly why the reverse can be learned — the true answer at each step is known because the corruption was applied deliberately. A VAE is the architecture that learns both directions.

stem: Select the architectures this course places on the generative side of the arc rather than on the predictive side or the representation bridge.
choices: Transformer
Convolutional neural network
Diffusion model
Multilayer perceptron
U-Net
explanation: Transformer and diffusion are the generative pair. MLP and CNN are predictive; U-Net sits on the bridge with the VAE, learning a representation that serves both prediction and generation.

stem: What is the key takeaway the course draws from putting all six architectures on one arc?
choices: Each architecture replaced the one before it, so only the newest is worth learning
The same core idea — neural networks that learn useful representations — powers both predictive and generative AI, and each architecture adds one new capability on top of it
The six are entirely separate inventions that happen to be taught together
Generative architectures are simply predictive architectures with more parameters
explanation: One foundation, six capabilities. Nothing was abandoned along the way: a diffusion model still contains a CNN, and a transformer still learns by gradient descent, which is why the arc runs from understanding the world to creating new possibilities.

stem: One word: name the 2014 architecture whose two networks compete, and which gave 'generative' its modern popular meaning before GPT took the word over.
explanation: The GAN, Generative Adversarial Network, from Goodfellow and colleagues in 2014. It was built to sharpen a discriminator and ended up the star, and deepfakes are what made it famous.

stem: Why can a generative model not be scored on accuracy the way a classifier is?
choices: Because its outputs are too large to compare automatically
Because there is no verifiable ground truth for an output that was never supposed to match anything; a newly generated face is judged on plausible context relevance instead
Because generative models are never trained on labelled data
Because accuracy is only defined for numeric outputs
explanation: There is nothing to be accurate against. Predictive AI is judged on accuracy against verifiable ground truths; generative AI is judged on whether the output is plausible and relevant to its context, which is a weaker and more slippery standard.

stem: Which architecture would you reach for to convert photographs of summer landscapes into winter versions of the same scenes, without any matched pairs to learn from?
choices: A cycle GAN, because adversarial training can learn a mapping between two image collections that are not paired up example by example
A plain MLP, because it can learn any mapping from input to output
A classifier trained to tell summer from winter, run in reverse
A U-Net trained on the summer images alone
explanation: Unpaired image-to-image translation is what the cycle GAN was built for: two adversarial pairs plus the requirement that translating there and back returns the original. Without pairs there is no reconstruction target, so an ordinary encoder-decoder has nothing to train against.

stem: A generative image model produces a person with six fingers. Why is this the characteristic failure of generative AI rather than a bug?
choices: Because the training images were mislabelled
Because the model has no ground truth to check against and is optimising for plausibility, so an output can be locally convincing while globally wrong
Because the model ran out of denoising steps before it finished
Because the prompt did not specify the number of fingers
explanation: Plausible context relevance is the only standard the model is held to, and local plausibility is easier to achieve than global consistency. It is the same failure shape as a language model's confident invention of a fact.

stem: 'The same reality, different routes, the same goal' summarises the generative family. What is the shared assumption about the data that makes these routes work at all?
choices: That the data are uniformly distributed, so any point is as likely as any other
That the data are labelled, so a supervised signal always exists
That the data live on a low-dimensional, structured manifold, so there is a simple distribution a learnable mapping can connect them to
That the dataset is small enough to be memorised in full
explanation: Real images occupy a tiny, highly structured corner of all possible pixel arrangements. That is what makes it possible to map a simple distribution onto them, and it is the same assumption behind the autoencoder's bottleneck.

stem: One word: name the operation a diffusion model is trained to perform, removing a little of the corruption at each step.
explanation: Denoising. Only the reverse direction is learned: the forward noising is prescribed, which is what makes the true answer at each step known and turns generation into an ordinary supervised problem repeated many times.

stem: Generative models are described with a mapping to a simple distribution and a mapping back. Which direction is used to generate, and why is the other one there at all?
choices: The mapping to the simple distribution generates; the mapping back checks the result
Neither is used for generation; a discriminator does the generating
Both directions generate, and the results are averaged
The mapping back from the simple distribution to the data generates; the mapping to the simple distribution exists to set up a supervised learning task with known targets
explanation: The outward mapping sets the homework and the return mapping learns to solve it backwards. Because we chose or constructed the trip to the simple distribution, we know the right answer at every step and can train on it.

stem: For VAE, diffusion and flow matching, which parts are learned and which are chosen by the designer?
choices: The VAE learns both encoder and decoder; diffusion fixes the forward noising and learns the reverse denoiser; flow matching chooses the probability path and learns the vector field that transports along it
All three fix both directions and learn only the sampling step
All three learn both directions
The VAE fixes the encoder; diffusion learns both directions; flow matching fixes both
explanation: Same goal, three different divisions of labour. The rule of thumb: whatever the designer fixes is what supplies the known target the learner is trained against.

stem: Among the generative families, the GAN is treated as the exception. What makes it one?
choices: It cannot generate images, only classify them
It has no explicit mapping from data to a simple distribution at all — a discriminator supplies the training signal instead of a known target
It is the only one that needs labelled data
It is the only one with a latent space
explanation: VAE, diffusion and flow matching each construct a route from data to a simple distribution and learn the way back. The GAN skips that and learns the generator purely from an adversary's verdict, which is why it trains so differently and so unstably.

stem: In conditional generation, the prompt is described as where to navigate and the random draw as which possibility. What does that split explain?
choices: Why a longer prompt always produces a better image
Why the model needs a discriminator at generation time
Why prompts must be written in English
Why the same prompt run twice gives different pictures: the text steers the generator to a region of the possibility space, and the random draw picks one particular sample inside it
explanation: Semantics directs, randomness varies. The randomness is not a defect to be removed — it is what makes the model generative rather than a lookup, and the prompt is what stops it wandering anywhere at all.

stem: Natural images are said to occupy a tiny high-density region of an enormous pixel space. What caveat does the course attach to calling that region a manifold?
choices: That no such region exists and the claim is purely metaphorical
That it only applies to images, not to text or audio
That manifold is a useful modelling intuition, but the safer statement is a concentrated high-density data distribution rather than a proven low-dimensional linear subspace
That the region is actually most of the space, not a small part of it
explanation: Almost every possible arrangement of pixels is noise; real photographs cluster tightly. Calling that cluster a manifold helps you think, but the course is careful not to claim the geometry has been proved.

stem: A variational autoencoder is trained by maximising the ELBO. What do those letters stand for?
choices: Encoder-Latent Bayesian Optimiser
Evidence Lower Bound
Expected Loss Before Output
Entropy-Limited Backward Objective
explanation: Evidence Lower Bound. It splits into a reconstruction term that keeps the output close to the input and a regularisation term that keeps the latent close to the simple prior — the two competing halves of the VAE objective.

stem: A team can afford only one generative image model. What does each of the VAE and the diffusion model give up in choosing the other?
choices: The VAE gives up the ability to generate at all; diffusion gives up the ability to reconstruct
Neither gives anything up; they are interchangeable
The VAE gives up sample quality; the diffusion model gives up the compact latent code and explicit likelihood, and is slow because it must be run for many steps
The VAE gives up its encoder; the diffusion model gives up its decoder
explanation: The VAE's strength is a compact, structured latent representation you can inspect and interpolate in. Diffusion's strength is empirical sample quality, paid for in a long iterative sampling loop.

stem: The adversarial idea was described in class as a second question following a first. Which pair?
choices: First, can two models be trained at once? Second, can they be made to agree?

First, can a model look at a photograph of a person and produce the judgement that it is that person? Second, can another engine produce an image good enough that the first model judges it a real photograph of them?
First, can a model compress an image? Second, can it rebuild it?
First, can a model add noise to an image? Second, can it remove the noise again?
explanation: Recognition first, then generation measured against that recogniser. The judge was built as a predictive model, and turning it into a training signal for a generator is what makes the GAN both ironic and effective.

stem: What led the field from predictive AI to generative AI?
choices: The arrival of larger datasets alone, with no change in method
The abandonment of neural networks in favour of probabilistic models

Networks learned compact representations of what the data are, and once that representation existed the same machinery could be run the other way to produce new samples — prediction and generation share one engine
The discovery that accuracy is not a useful measure
explanation: The representation bridge is the hinge: VAE and U-Net learn the structure, and Transformer and Diffusion exploit it to generate. Nothing was thrown away — the universal approximator and gradient-based learning are the same underneath both.

stem: Generative AI is described as extrapolating beyond the basis of validation. Why is that both the source of its power and the source of its danger?
choices: Because it makes the model slower to run but more accurate
Because it needs more training data than a predictive model
Because extrapolation guarantees the output is novel and therefore always useful
Because it produces things no example in the data ever showed — which is what makes it creative, and also means there is no ground truth left to check the output against
explanation: A predictive model can be marked against a verifiable answer; a generated one cannot, because there was never a right answer to compare it with. Judging it therefore falls back on plausibility and context, and on the reader's own knowledge.
